content_voiceover: This slide reviews three board style questions with their answers marked. Question sixty two describes a patient with antiphospholipid syndrome, a markedly prolonged aPTT, and positivity for lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibody, and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I antibody, in other words triple positive APS, and asks the best choice for long term anticoagulation. The correct answer is C, vitamin K antagonist, directly reinforcing the point from a few slides back that DOACs underperform warfarin in triple positive antiphospholipid syndrome. Question sixty nine asks about DOAC interference in hemostasis assays across four statements, that PT may be prolonged with rivaroxaban and edoxaban, that dabigatran does not tend to prolong PT, that there is a false increase in clot based protein C and S activity, and that DRVVT based lupus anticoagulant assays may show false positive results. All four statements are actually true, so the correct answer is E, one plus two plus three plus four, and this highlights an important pitfall, DOACs can distort thrombophilia workups if testing is not timed or chosen carefully. Question fifty seven asks which vitamin K dependent clotting factor has the shortest plasma half life, and the answer is B, factor VII, at roughly four to six hours, which is exactly why PT and INR rise first after starting warfarin, before factors two, nine, and ten are sufficiently depleted.
keypoints: Triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome should be anticoagulated with a vitamin K antagonist
DOACs can falsely raise clot-based protein C and S activity and cause false-positive DRVVT results
Dabigatran typically does not prolong PT, but rivaroxaban and edoxaban can
Factor VII has the shortest half-life among vitamin K-dependent factors, explaining early INR rise
keypoint_voiceover: Remember, triple positive antiphospholipid syndrome calls for a vitamin K antagonist, not a DOAC. DOACs can falsely raise clot based protein C and S activity and produce false positive DRVVT lupus anticoagulant results, and dabigatran typically spares the PT while rivaroxaban and edoxaban can prolong it. Finally, factor VII has the shortest half life among vitamin K dependent factors, which is why INR rises first on warfarin.
